title: main-sync git-merge-main uses --no-ff so a diverged branch can sync, and its failure path is transactional

sha_binding.verified_source_note: Last commit on this branch touching a non-proof path (round-10 remediation: the bisect enumeration and the measured release prose). merge_sha is null pre-merge as the shared evidence schema requires.

verified_source_sha_history.superseded_reason: Round-1 head. Superseded by the P1 remediation commit: the --no-ff change made a conflicting merge reachable, and the wrapper failure path popped the lane-state autostash and released the merge mutex while MERGE_HEAD and unmerged index entries were still in the worktree.

Round-2 head. Superseded by the round-3 remediation commit: independent review found that abortInProgressSync collapsed an undeterminable probe result into 'the ref is absent', so a repository that could not answer took the 'nothing to abort' early return and the wrapper popped the autostash and released the mutex anyway -- the same fail-open class as the P1, one layer down; and that the caller-supplied onCommandFailure hook was called unguarded, so a throwing hook escaped runMergeWrapper with the lock held and no structured result.

Round-3 head. Superseded by the round-4 remediation commit: an independent reviewer demonstrated that the round-3 proof asserted the fail-closed message 'names the git command that actually ran' when commandVector rendered the bridged `git pull --ff-only origin main` instead -- a command that cannot leave MERGE_HEAD behind -- and that three further controls (the abort verb, the not-attempted stash pop, and the unmerged-paths term of the early return) were pinned by no test or mutant.

Round-4 head. Superseded by the round-5 remediation commit: an independent reviewer demonstrated by execution a fail-open that this bundle certified as impossible -- after a SUCCESSFUL merge, a conflicting `git stash pop` leaves unmerged index entries and conflict markers and the wrapper released the merge mutex anyway -- plus an unpinned third term of `residue` (an undeterminable POST-abort state read clean), and three mutation rows (M1/M2/M3) carried forward from round 3 while corroboration claimed all twelve were measured against the current source.

verified_source_sha_history.note: round-6 remediation: measured release decisions, stash-push fail-closed, head-move notice reachability
round-7 remediation: probe bound to every delegation, sequencer states covered, protected-path restore on the failed path, dead override removed

verified_source_sha_history.superseded_reason: Round-7 head. Superseded by the round-8 remediation commit: an independent reviewer demonstrated by execution that round 7's sequencer-state terms (rebase-merge/rebase-apply directory, CHERRY_PICK_HEAD, REVERT_HEAD) were wired only into branches reachable from an unmerged index, while every sequencer state leaves the index clean -- so the terms were unreachable from every production decision path and main-sync over a mid-rebase worktree still ran `git pull --ff-only`, fast-forwarded the detached HEAD out from under the rebase, reported merge_wrapper_completed and released the repo-wide merge mutex. NOTE: this SHA no longer exists on the branch; see sha_rewrite_record below.

Round-8 head. Superseded by the round-9 remediation commit: an independent reviewer proved by execution that the round-8 pre-flight, which sits after acquireMergeLock, retained the repo-wide merge mutex on a refusal that had changed nothing -- so any probe-less caller acquired the serializing lock, did nothing, and never released it for the full TTL, and the reviewer blocked its own next sanctioned command with it. The round-8 bundle had disclosed that code path and asserted 'no safety property regresses', which was false. The same review found evidence.json's mutants[] array left at round-7 data, recording the known survivor M16 as KILLED and omitting M23-M26. NOTE: this SHA no longer exists on the branch; see sha_rewrite_record.

sha_rewrite_record.why: Governed remediation, in four passes. (1) commit 9162d2c9's BODY contained the token `(UTV2-1678)`, which the branch-discipline guard scans for and rejects on a UTV2-1790 branch; removing it rewrote that commit and every commit after it. (2) a descendant SUBJECT cited 9162d2c9 by SHA and was repointed. (3) round 9 found the round-8 rewrite had fixed that subject but MISSED a commit BODY that still cited 9162d2c9, so the claim 'no message names a commit that is not on it' was false when first written; it was repointed too. (4) fixing (3) renamed the next commit in turn and invalidated ITS SHA-bearing subject, so the SHA was removed from that subject rather than repointed. The durable lesson: a SHA in a commit subject is self-invalidating under any message rewrite. Verified after the final pass: every hex token in every commit message on this branch that resolves to a commit is an ancestor of HEAD.
sha_rewrite_record.trees_unchanged: Verified, with the round-9 correction to the evidence cited. The invariant tip tree across the rewrites is d1227506 (the tree of cb059ebb and of its rewritten twin 4a766873). Round 8 cited fd554012 here, which is the tree of a commit created AFTER both rewrites and therefore could not have existed before them -- the claim was true but the evidence for it was wrong, and a round-9 reviewer caught it. The reviewer independently verified all six old->new mappings byte-identical. Only commit messages changed; no content, no author and no authored timestamp was altered.

verdict.mutex_acquire_release_preserved: QUALIFIED — the safety invariant is preserved; the release SITE is deliberately moved by this lane. Round 5 recorded this as a flat true while round 5 was itself relocating the release, and round 6 recorded it as flat true while a stash-push failure still released over a conflicted index. It is now: released after a successful merge, after a cleanly-aborted failing one, and after a non-conflicting pop failure over a MEASURED-clean tree; retained on cleanup failure, on a conflicting pop, on a stash-push failure over an in-progress merge, and whenever the tree could not be measured.  Round 7 extended this to `main-sync`, which had never received the probe at all and therefore leaked the mutex on every failed pop. Tests 27, 48, 49, 51, 52, 55, 56, 57, 58, 59, 60, 61.
verdict.head_move_invalidation_reporting_preserv: QUALIFIED — the reporting primitives are untouched, but this lane created a path that reached the post-sync analysis with ok:false after a COMMITTED merge (merge_wrapper_stash_pop_conflict), and the `!result.ok` early return skipped both classifyDroppedPaths and renderHeadMoveNotice on it. Reachability repaired in round 6: a failed result keeps its code and the notice is appended to its stderr. Test 57, mutant M18.
verdict.statement: git-merge-main built `git merge --ff-only origin/main`, which cannot merge a diverged branch by definition, so main-sync's recommended exit for divergence failed on exactly the condition it exists for -- leaving git-rebase-main, which rewrites history and invalidates every head-pinned governance artifact, as the only operable path. The command is now `git merge --no-ff --no-edit origin/main`: it merges a genuinely diverged branch while preserving both sides' commit SHAs byte-for-byte, is deliberately not a bare `git merge` (which would fast-forward a merely-behind branch and make the verb's effect depend on divergence state), and is noninteractive. Permitting a non-fast-forward merge also permits a conflicting one, which exposed a second defect on the same path and was raised as a review P1: the wrapper popped its lane-state autostash and released the merge mutex while MERGE_HEAD and unmerged index entries were still present, stranding lane state in the stash and letting the next lane acquire a mutex over a half-merged worktree. The failure path is now transactional: abortInProgressSync aborts the in-progress merge/rebase and verifies the result before the stash is restored and before the lock is released, and a cleanup that cannot restore the pre-attempt state fails closed with the distinct merge_wrapper_cleanup_failed code, the mutex retained and the stash left intact. All five wrapper safety invariants are preserved; the mutex ordering is hardened, not weakened. Round 3 closed two fail-open residuals found by independent review: an undeterminable probe result (git exit 128) was being read as 'the ref is absent', which sent an unreadable repository down the 'nothing to abort' early return; and the caller-supplied onCommandFailure hook was called unguarded, so a throwing hook escaped runMergeWrapper with the lock held and no structured result. Both now force the fail-closed branch. The fail-closed recovery message also named `pnpm ops:merge-wrapper guard`, which only asserts the lock is held; it now names `pnpm ops:merge-lock release`. Round 4 corrected a FALSE claim that round 3's proof made and three controls that nothing pinned, all found by a second independent reviewer. The false claim: the fail-closed message was asserted to name the git command that actually ran, but commandVector was built from the bridged input, so it rendered `git pull --ff-only origin main` -- an invocation that cannot leave MERGE_HEAD behind -- and pointed the operator away from the residue. runMergeWrapper now takes a reportedCommand option: what is run is still `command`, what is reported is the caller's real vector. The three unpinned controls were the abort verb (hardcoding `merge` survived the whole suite; `git merge --abort` during a rebase exits 128 and the residue survives), the not-attempted autostash pop (test 49's assertions were satisfied by git's own refusal to pop into an unmerged index, not by the control), and the unmerged-paths term of the nothing-to-abort early return. Each is now pinned by a test and a mutant (M9-M12). Round 5 closed a fail-open that round 4's proof certified as impossible. Every prior regression entered through the command FAILURE path; this one enters through the SUCCESS path -- the merge completes, `git stash pop` then conflicts because the commit just merged from main touches an autostashed path, and the wrapper released the serializing mutex over a worktree carrying unmerged entries and conflict markers. The release now happens after that branch and the branch returns without releasing. Round 5 also pinned the third term of `residue` (an undeterminable POST-abort state was read as clean, killed by nothing until M13) and re-measured every mutation row: M1/M2/M3 had been carried forward from round 3 at 7/3/5 while the suite grew, and are 10/4/8 against the current source.
verdict.mutex_released_only_after_cleanup_succee: Round 4 asserted this true while a counterexample existed on the SUCCESS path: a conflicting autostash pop left unmerged entries and the mutex was released anyway. Round 5 fixed the code, so the field is true as of 9162d2c9 -- but it was certified before it was proven, and that is recorded in finding 11 rather than quietly corrected.
verdict.protected_artifact_dropped_by_a_failed_s: IMPLEMENTED BUT UNPINNED -- no regression stands behind this branch. classifyDroppedPaths compares origin/main...preSyncHead against origin/main..HEAD, so a drop means the sync LOST the lane its own work: it needs a rebase that silently drops a lane commit AND a stash-pop failure in the same run. Every fixture attempted either classified nothing as dropped or would have asserted the restore of a file that was never lost. Recorded as unpinned rather than covered by a vacuous test.
verdict.residue_definition_is_an_enumeration_not: Round 10, P1: git bisect was absent from the enumeration, so a bisecting worktree read clean and main-sync fast-forwarded its detached HEAD off the commit under test while returning merge_wrapper_completed. Eight candidate in-progress states were then built against real git and measured; only bisect was invisible. A .git/sequencer term was considered and REJECTED as an equivalent mutant -- no state was found that it catches and CHERRY_PICK_HEAD/REVERT_HEAD/unmerged paths do not. The enumeration is now MERGE_HEAD, REBASE_HEAD, rebase-merge/rebase-apply, CHERRY_PICK_HEAD, REVERT_HEAD, BISECT_LOG/BISECT_START and unmerged paths, threaded into all three consumers. It remains an enumeration, and that residual is recorded in known_gaps.

mutants.name: ['merge','--no-ff','--no-edit','origin/main'] -> ['merge','--ff-only','origin/main']
mutants.note: Killed behaviourally, not only by shape: 47-50 fail because the merge genuinely does not occur under --ff-only against a real diverged repository.

mutants.name: --no-edit removed
mutants.note: Killed by command-shape assertions ONLY. git merge --no-ff opens $GIT_EDITOR only when run from a terminal and the wrapper spawns git with piped stdio, so --no-edit cannot be made behaviourally load-bearing in this harness. It is the guarantee for tty callers; the shape assertion pins it.

mutants.name: onCommandFailure wiring removed from the sync path
mutants.note: Reproduces the reviewed P1 exactly: a conflicted merge again releases the mutex and attempts the autostash pop with MERGE_HEAD and unmerged entries still present.

mutants.name: abortInProgressSync failure return reports cleaned: true
mutants.note: Proves the fail-closed `cleaned` computation is load-bearing: a tree that could not be cleaned must never be reported clean.

mutants.name: the `if (cleanup && !cleanup.cleaned)` fail-closed branch removed, so the wrapper pops and releases anyway
mutants.note: Proves the fail-closed branch must exist at all.

mutants.name: a BEFORE-abort undeterminable probe treated as absence (`if (before.undetermined.length > 0)` -> `if (false)`)
mutants.note: Reproduces the reviewed round-2 P2 exactly: collapsing 'the probe could not answer' into 'the ref is absent' sends an undeterminable tree down the 'nothing to abort' early return, pops the autostash into a possibly-unmerged index and releases the mutex.

mutants.name: the try/catch around the onCommandFailure call removed, so a throwing hook escapes
mutants.note: Proves the hook boundary is guarded: without it a throwing caller-supplied hook exits runMergeWrapper with the lock held, the stash unpopped and no structured result.

mutants.name: the mutex released anyway inside the fail-closed branch, before returning
mutants.note: Proves the fail-closed branch must not release the mutex on its way out.

mutants.name: reportedCommand removed, so results name the bridged main-sync pull
mutants.note: Round 4. Reproduces the reviewed P2 exactly: the fail-closed result names `git pull --ff-only origin main`, a command that cannot leave MERGE_HEAD behind, pointing the operator away from the residue.

mutants.name: the abort verb hardcoded to 'merge' regardless of operation
mutants.note: Round 4. `git merge --abort` during a rebase exits 128 and the residue survives. It fails closed rather than open, but it converts automatic recovery into a manual-recovery incident for git-rebase-main. Survived the entire 52-test suite before test 53 existed.

mutants.name: a `git stash pop` attempted inside the fail-closed branch
mutants.note: Round 4. Test 49's `popped === false` and 'stash entry still listed' were satisfied by git's own refusal to pop into an unmerged index, so they passed under this mutant; the test now asserts the call was never issued.

mutants.name: `after.undetermined.length > 0` dropped from `residue`, so an unverifiable POST-abort state reads clean
mutants.note: Round 5. Pinned by nothing before test 56: test 51 masks ALL probes, so the before-probe fail-closed fires first and the after-probe is never exercised. Without this term the wrapper pops the autostash into a still-conflicted index and releases the mutex.

mutants.name: the mutex released on a conflicting autostash pop
mutants.note: Round 5, the reviewed P1. Reproduces the fail-open exactly: after a SUCCESSFUL merge a conflicting `git stash pop` leaves unmerged entries and conflict markers, and the serializing mutex is handed to the next lane over that worktree.

mutants.name: the mutex NEVER released on a failed `git stash pop` (round-5 behaviour restored: `const release = false`)
mutants.note: Round-6 P1. The deliberate opposite of M14: M14 proves the lock must be RETAINED over a conflicted index, M15 proves it must be RELEASED over a measured-clean one. Only a measurement distinguishes them, which is exactly why round 5's unmeasured retention read as safe.

mutants.name: the mutex released unconditionally on a stash-PUSH failure (pre-fix behaviour)
mutants.note: SURVIVOR. Round 8 moved the enforcing control earlier: main-sync now measures the worktree BEFORE the autostash, so the stranded-merge scenario is caught by the pre-flight and this later branch is no longer the control that carries it. NOT deleted -- unlike round 7's dead residueProbe override it is not provably equivalent to its surroundings, since the tree could in principle change between the two measurements -- so it remains as defence-in-depth and is declared a survivor. The residue probe is an ENUMERATION, not a general 'is git mid-operation' predicate, and round 10 showed what that costs: a state absent from the list is invisible, and invisible means the pre-flight passes it. The list is now MERGE_HEAD, REBASE_HEAD, rebase-merge/rebase-apply, CHERRY_PICK_HEAD, REVERT_HEAD, BISECT_LOG/BISECT_START and unmerged paths. Eight candidate states were built against real git and measured to close the round-10 hole rather than patch it, and only bisect was missing -- but that sweep is a snapshot of git as it is today, not a proof of completeness. A future git operation that detaches HEAD and leaves state outside those files would reproduce this class again. The durable fix would be to ask git for its own answer (there is no single porcelain that reports it) rather than to restate the list; that is out of scope for a blocker fix and is the strongest argument for keeping the refusal fail-closed on any unmeasurable state.

The round-10 P3 fix makes the pre-flight's prose follow `release.ok`, but the release attempt itself is still made unconditionally and a failed release still leaves the lock held by another owner. The wrapper reports that truthfully and does not attempt to reclaim it; reclaiming another owner's lock is exactly what the mutex exists to prevent. The operator must resolve it, which is why the message now names the failure code.
